# BCrypt Crypto Only, No Spring Security

**Decision.** Take `spring-security-crypto` for its BCrypt password encoder and **nothing else** from
Spring Security. Authentication is a hand-written interceptor over jjwt.

**Date.** 2026-05-28, lab 4 of `Information-Systems-Modelling`.

## The decision is a comment in the build file

> "<!-- BCrypt password hashing (no full Spring Security pulled in) -->"
> — Information-Systems-Modelling/lab4/StudentService/pom.xml, 2026-05-28

Twelve words in a `pom.xml`, and they are doing real work: `spring-security-crypto` is a small
standalone jar with no auto-configuration, whereas `spring-boot-starter-security` would lock down
every endpoint by default, install a filter chain, and change the shape of the whole application.
The comment exists because the *next* reader will otherwise see `org.springframework.security` in the
dependency list and assume the framework is in play.

## What was built instead

| Class | Role |
|---|---|
| `JwtService` | issue / verify tokens — jjwt 0.12.6, HMAC-SHA, 24 h TTL |
| `AuthInterceptor` | Spring MVC `HandlerInterceptor`, registered in `WebMvcConfig.addInterceptors` |
| `CurrentUser` | the resolved principal handed to controllers |

Plus `passwordEncoder.encode(...)` in `UserServiceImpl.register` and `verifyCredentials(...)` on
login. That is the entire authentication system — see [[stateless-jwt-authentication]].

## The rejected alternative, and the trade actually made

`spring-boot-starter-security` would have supplied, for free: a filter chain that runs *before*
Spring MVC, CSRF handling, a session-fixation strategy, `@PreAuthorize` method-level authorisation,
a standard `UserDetailsService` contract, and security-aware test slices.

What the hand-rolled version gives up is mostly the first item. **An interceptor runs inside Spring
MVC's dispatch, a security filter runs before it** — so anything served outside the
`DispatcherServlet` mapping, or any handler path not covered by the interceptor's registration, is
simply unguarded. The authorisation surface becomes "whatever is listed in `WebMvcConfig`" rather
than "deny by default". With Actuator also on the classpath in lab 4, that is a real difference and
not a theoretical one.

What it buys is legibility: the whole auth path is three readable classes with no
auto-configuration, no filter-order puzzles and nothing to un-configure. For a lab whose grading
depends on the reader following the mechanism, that is a defensible call.

## Not verified

**No test covers any of it.** The interceptor's exclusion list, token expiry, a tampered signature, a
missing header and role checks are all untested; lab 4's Java suite is one `contextLoads()` plus one
integration test. A pointcut-style registration list that silently stops matching fails open, which
is the specific hazard this design creates. See [[tests-that-pass-for-the-wrong-reason]].

Related, and worse in the ancestor: **lab 3 has neither this dependency nor any of these classes**,
while its README and OpenAPI contract both promise bcrypt-backed JWT auth. The decision recorded here
is what made lab 4 real. See [[forward-copy-lab-progression]].
